newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 28.

text.p: A Court ruling on Thursday that Maoris are allowed to fish without a licence for trout in their tribal area may be appealed against. Fish and Game NZ director Bryce Johnson said the decision, by a Wanganui judge, was a concern to anglers. A legal opinion of the decision would be sought and it might be appealed against. Page 1.

A growing number of National MPs are publicly voicing their opposition to compulsory superannuation. Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters did nothing to bring them on side on Thursday when he failed to rule out an abatement regime that would cut entitlement to state pensions as compulsory private provisions grew. A binding $10 million referendum on compulsory superannuation is to be held in September. Page 1.

The high-powered Parliamentary Service Commission has decided to investigate options to bulk-fund MPs as calls emerge for greater financial accountability on MPs' expenses and for the travel perks of former MPs to be scrapped. Bulk funding would mean MPs would be given a limited sum to cover all their expenses, and could decide within that budget what to spend it on. Page 2.

NZ First leader Winston Peters started a ferocious attack against opposition MPs on Thursday, slating everything from their hairstyles to their sleeping habits. His speech left Labour struggling to retaliate in a robust address-in-reply debate that was frequently interrupted by the Speaker's calls to MPs to tone down their behaviour. Page 2.

Cabinet ministers were warned that the price of video equipment and facilities to be bought by Aotearoa Television Network would rise if the broadcaster got more government funding, a Commerce Ministry paper shows. The paper, obtained by

the Labour Party under the Official Information Act, also says that "indications are that at least two of the directors -- and possibly all of them -- were paid $50,000 each for each three-month period". Page 2.

Foreign Minister Don McKinnon has ended a round of meetings in Washington, confident that New Zealand's relations with the United States are progressing. "New Zealand's relations with the United States are the best they've been in more than a decade," McKinnon said on Thursday. Page 2.

The government would move a resolution next Tuesday for the setting up of select committees, Leader of the House Wyatt Creech said on Thursday. On Wednesday, the first general debate and first private member's bills would be heard. It is expected that National will chair most select committees, with NZ First chairing one and ACT NZ chairing another. Page 2.

The government reported a NZ$1.94 billion surplus on its operations in the six months to December in 1996, $323 million more than forecast and in line with analysts' expectations. Economists said the data had little impact on the financial records and was in an exceptionally strong position. Page 12.

Listed publisher Wilson and Horton made a $40.1 million after-tax profit for the year ended December 31, the company reported. The result, achieved on sales of $445.49 million, compares with an after-tax profit of $35.69 million reported for the nine months to December 31, 1995. Page 12.

Macraes Mining has reported a more-than-doubled profit for the 1996 calendar year, while more than halving its final dividend to fund future expansion. Net profit of $15.44 million was 118 percent higher than 1995's $7.09 million, but the dividend of two cents a share was down from five cents. Sky Television has stepped up the competition for pay-TV customers by providing satellite dishes to New Zealand homes that can't get the conventional UHF reception. Sky chief executive Nate Smith said in Auckland on Thursday that the move, along with progressive delivery of more channels, was expected to attract a further 40,000 viewers -- using either the satellite dishes or the existing UHF transmission. Page 12.

A high-powered French business delegation in Wellington on Thursday was "very interested" in New Zealand's economic revolution, and that might encourage more business between the two countries, delegation leader Claude Bebear said. Bebear and 12 other business leaders, representing companies from telecommunications and aircraft to film-making and tourism, met Prime Minister Jim Bolger, Treasurer Winston Peters and Finance Minister Bill Birch. Page 12.
